Table 1 explicitly includes two baseline MDZ components from Espejo et al. (2016): Experiment 1 (Fig. 1, 5-min reactivation, 3 mg/kg MDZ, Ntotal = 15, d = 4.05) and Experiment 2 (Fig. 2, 5-min reactivation, 3 mg/kg MDZ, Ntotal = 22, d = 3.03). A separate housing study mentioned in Discussion (Schroyens, Bender, et al., 2019) does not negate the conceptual replication experiments reported here. These newly collected cohorts (164 rats) are independent of shipped row 2487 (Alfei et al., 2015, Lab IV) and other Lab I studies.

decision.reason: In Methods 2.9.6 and Discussion Section 4, the current paper explicitly cites Gazarini et al. (2015) alongside Bustos et al. (2010), Espejo et al. (2016, 2017), and Ortiz et al. (2015) for the empirical finding that systemic administration of the NMDA partial agonist D-cycloserine (DCS, 15 mg/kg i.p., 30 min before contextual fear reactivation) enables destabilization of otherwise resistant contextual fear memories so that post-reactivation amnestic treatment interferes with reconsolidation, and directly contrasts current experiments NS12 and NS20 against that cited set. The complete primary text of Gazarini et al. (2015) confirms that Experiment 5 (Fig. 5B, N = 51 adult male Wistar rats, 7-9/group) empirically tested systemic pre-retrieval DCS (15 mg/kg i.p., 30 min before a 3-min contextual retrieval session) followed immediately by post-retrieval reconsolidation blockers (clonidine 0.3 mg/kg or cannabidiol 10 mg/kg i.p.) in rats with yohimbine-induced reconsolidation-resistant contextual fear memories, finding significant fear reduction at test (F(5,45) = 9.0, p < 0.00001). Under the codebook, differences in resistance induction (standard/3-day training vs yohimbine) and post-retrieval blocker (MDZ vs clonidine/CBD) do not exclude conceptual retesting of the pre-retrieval DCS destabilization-facilitation finding. Gazarini et al. (2015) is absent from shipped row 2487 and all other targets.
